name: The Intentional Fallacy
statement: Judging a work by what the author intended is a mistake: the meaning is in the text, not the mind.
statementAccent: the meaning is in the text
meaning: The intentional fallacy is the alleged error of judging or interpreting a work of art, especially a literary work, by appeal to the author's intention, what the author meant or set out to do. The underlying thesis, anti-intentionalism, is that the design or intention of the author is neither available nor desirable as a standard for judging the success of a work of literary art; the meaning and value of the work are properties of the work itself, publicly available in the text, not of the author's private mental states or aims. The term and argument come from William K. Wimsatt and Monroe C. Beardsley in their essay The Intentional Fallacy, published in 1946 in the Sewanee Review and reprinted in Wimsatt's 1954 book The Verbal Icon, and they are associated with the New Criticism, which emphasized close reading of the text itself and the autonomy of the work. Wimsatt and Beardsley pressed a dilemma: if the poet succeeded, the poem itself shows the intention, so appeal to external evidence of it is unnecessary; if the poet failed, the external evidence of intention does not count as part of the work, so it is not a proper standard. They distinguished internal evidence, in the work and public, part of its meaning, from external evidence, such as the author's letters and stated aims, private and not part of the work. Their companion essay, The Affective Fallacy of 1949, targets judging a poem by its emotional effects on the reader.
mechanism: The intentional fallacy argument turns on where the meaning and value of a literary work reside. Wimsatt and Beardsley hold that a poem, once made, belongs to the public and goes about the world beyond the author's power to intend about it or control it; its meaning is embodied in the words on the page, which are shareable and open to analysis, rather than in the author's inner purposes, which are private and idiosyncratic. From this they draw their central dilemma about the relevance of authorial intention to evaluating a work. Either the poet realized the intention in the poem, in which case the poem itself displays what was intended and we need not, and should not, appeal to anything outside it; or the poet failed to realize the intention, in which case the discrepancy between what was intended and what was achieved is a fact about the author's mind that does not belong to the poem, so citing it cannot be a legitimate standard for judging the poem. Either way, external intention drops out as a criterion. This supports a distinction between kinds of evidence: internal evidence, drawn from the semantic and formal features of the work, its language, images, and structure, is public and constitutive of meaning, whereas external evidence, such as the author's diaries, letters, and declarations of aim, is private and, on the anti-intentionalist view, not part of what the work means. The New Critics built on this a practice of close reading that treats the text as an autonomous object. The Affective Fallacy makes a parallel move at the other end, arguing that judging a poem by its results in the reader confuses the poem with its effects.

examples.text: Wimsatt and Beardsley held the author's intention is neither available nor desirable as a standard for judging a work.
If the poet succeeded the poem shows the intention; if the poet failed, external intention is not part of the work either.
Evidence in the text is public and part of meaning; the author's letters and stated aims are private and external to it.

variants.name: The affective fallacy
variants.text: The companion error of judging a poem by its emotional effects on the reader, confusing the poem with its results.

variants.name: Later intentionalisms
variants.text: Actual and hypothetical intentionalism, which restore a role for the author's actual or best-hypothesized intention.

whyItMatters: The intentional fallacy is one of the most influential ideas in twentieth-century criticism and the philosophy of art, and it reshaped how literature and art are read and taught. By arguing that a work's meaning and value lie in the text itself rather than in the author's private intentions, Wimsatt and Beardsley gave the New Criticism its methodological charter, licensing the practice of close reading that treats the poem as an autonomous verbal object to be analyzed on its own terms, a practice that dominated literary study for decades. The essay sharpened the crucial distinction between the meaning a work publicly bears and the aims its maker happened to have, a distinction that bears on interpretation, evaluation, and the very locus of meaning in art. It provoked an enduring debate: actual intentionalists such as E. D. Hirsch defended authorial intention as determining meaning, hypothetical intentionalists such as Jerrold Levinson appealed to the best hypothesis about the author's intent, and the poststructuralist death of the author, announced by Roland Barthes, pushed anti-intentionalism further still. Whether one accepts or rejects it, the intentional fallacy set the terms for thinking about authorship, meaning, and interpretation. As the claim that the author's intention is not the measure of the work, it is a landmark of modern aesthetics and criticism.

working.text: hold that a work's meaning and value are public properties of the work, not of the author's private mind.
note that if intention succeeded the text shows it, and if it failed, external intention is not part of the work.
treat internal textual evidence as constitutive of meaning and external biographical evidence as outside it.

limits: The intentional fallacy is contested, and many philosophers reject or qualify it. Actual intentionalists argue that the author's intention is, at least in part, what fixes a work's meaning, since interpretation aims at understanding a communicative act, and E. D. Hirsch, in his 1967 Validity in Interpretation, defended authorial intention as the determinant of verbal meaning. Hypothetical intentionalists, such as Jerrold Levinson, offer a middle path on which meaning is fixed by the best hypothesis about the author's intention formed by a suitably informed audience, giving intention a role without making the author's private avowals decisive. Critics also note that the sharp internal-external distinction is hard to draw, since context, conventions, and knowledge of the author's language and situation, arguably external, are routinely and legitimately used in interpretation. The poststructuralist tradition, by contrast, radicalized anti-intentionalism with Barthes's death of the author. Some historical details reward care: the essay appeared in 1946 in the Sewanee Review and was reprinted in The Verbal Icon in 1954, the companion Affective Fallacy in 1949, and there is no single dedicated encyclopedia entry under the exact name. So the intentional fallacy robustly locates meaning in the work rather than the author's mind, understood as an influential but disputed thesis challenged by actual and hypothetical intentionalism.
misreadings: The intentional fallacy is not the claim that authors have no intentions or that intentions never matter to making art; it is the claim that the author's intention is not the standard for the meaning and value of the finished work. It does not forbid all use of context, only the appeal to private, external evidence of aim as a criterion, and where that line falls is disputed. And anti-intentionalism is not uncontested, since actual and hypothetical intentionalists restore a role for intention, so treating the intentional fallacy as denying authorial intention exists, as banning all context, or as settled doctrine, misreads it.
origin: The thesis, argued by Wimsatt and Beardsley in their 1946 essay The Intentional Fallacy and central to the New Criticism, that a work's meaning and value lie in the text itself rather than in the author's private intention.
